title: Naturita Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Naturita wells have a 104 ft median depth, with typical completed well costs of $11,200-$19,800.
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Naturita means looking past the existence of a well permit. The local records show a wide range of depths, mostly fractured-bedrock wells, and limited reported pump and water-level data. Within 5 miles of Naturita, Colorado DWR records include 469 permitted wells, but only 169 are recorded as constructed.

This guide uses the available records to explain what a buyer may encounter around Naturita, Nucla, and nearby Montrose County properties. Treat the statistics as planning information, not a guarantee for a particular lot. A driller still needs to evaluate the exact parcel, access, geology, casing and grout requirements, and the intended household use.

sections.heading: Naturita well depth depends on the ground below the lot
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Naturita is 104 feet. The middle half runs from 21 to 240 feet, which is a very broad spread for estimating a new well. Nearly half of the reported wells are under 100 feet, while 34% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 16% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 2% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 640 feet.

Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 425 wells in that category. That geology can change quickly over short distances. For a drilling bid, the 104-foot median is a useful starting point, but the 21-to-240-foot middle range matters more than the median alone. Ask for a written estimate that explains what happens if the hole must go deeper.

sections.heading: What Naturita wells produce for household use
sections.html:
Only 23 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are useful but not highly certain for every neighborhood. Among those reports, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 7.5 to 12.5 gallons per minute. Seventy percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 22% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, and 9% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. That is encouraging for basic household planning, but a reported yield is not the same as guaranteed storage or sustained production. Confirm the well’s permit limits, pump setting, pressure tank, and any required testing before assuming it will support irrigation, livestock, or a larger home.

sections.heading: The water-level record is too thin to show a trend
sections.html:
Four wells report a static water level, with a median depth to water of 125 feet and a middle half from 39 to 205 feet. That range is large enough to affect pump selection, trenching, and the cost of bringing water into a home. It also shows why a nearby well’s water level can be more useful than a countywide assumption.

There are not enough reported static measurements to establish a reliable water-table trend by decade around Naturita. Do not treat the available records as proof that groundwater is falling or stable. Before buying, obtain the well construction report and recent pumping information for the property, then have a qualified driller evaluate drawdown, pump placement, and recovery.

sections.heading: Recent permits show active drilling around Naturita
sections.html:
The permit history is not limited to older rural homes. Records show 150 permits issued in the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2024. Earlier totals include 70 in the 2010s, 35 in the 2000s, and 87 in the 1990s. The records also include 28 permits from the 1970s and 25 from the 1980s.

The most frequently listed drillers are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 74 records; Gordon Smith And Company, with 21; and Smith Drilling C/O Gordon R. Smith, with 13. These names describe permit records, not a recommendation. Verify current licensing, insurance, references, and availability. A permit is not proof that a well was completed, since 469 permits appear in the broader record but only 169 are marked constructed.

sections.heading: A Naturita well can cost more than the hole itself
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground modeled around Naturita, the typical drilling rate is $50 to $75 per foot. Applied to the 104-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $5,200 to $7,800. That figure is only the drilling portion and should not be mistaken for a complete water system.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $11,200 to $19,800 at the median depth. A property with a deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, additional casing or grout, or longer utility runs can cost more. Request an itemized bid that separates drilling, casing, grouting, development, pump equipment, electrical work, trenching, and testing.

sections.heading: Naturita buyers should check water quality and the building site
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information deserves a closer look before closing. Within about 10 miles, the records show 14 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 135 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. These maps do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are good reasons to order a laboratory water test and review the property’s distance from mines, waste areas, and other known sites.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured bedrock even when nearby wells produce water. Also confirm separation between the well, septic system, reserve leach area, property boundaries, and the proposed building site. Septic approval and a well permit are separate issues. Ask the county and Colorado DWR what the permit allows; an exempt household-use well generally has a 35 gpm pumping limit, and some basins require augmentation plans.

sections.heading: Before buying or building near Naturita
sections.html:
Start with the exact permit number and construction report, not just a listing description. Compare the property’s depth, yield, static water level, pump test, and water-quality results with nearby records in Naturita and Nucla. If you are looking farther out toward Redvale or Norwood, do not assume the same geology or costs apply.

For a vacant lot, make the well location, septic layout, access road, electrical route, and building envelope part of the early site plan. Confirm that drilling equipment can reach the location and that the road can support construction traffic. For an existing home, test the water, inspect the pressure system, and verify that the recorded well matches the equipment and actual use. A local driller can price risk more accurately after seeing the parcel.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Naturita, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Naturita is 104 feet. The middle half runs from 21 to 240 feet, while the deepest record reaches 640 feet. Nearly half are under 100 feet, but fractured-bedrock conditions can change quickly, so a nearby well is useful evidence rather than a guarantee for a new hole.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Naturita?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate near Naturita is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 104-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $5,200 to $7,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $11,200 to $19,800. Deeper drilling, difficult access, and site-specific construction requirements can increase the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Naturita?
faq.a: Only 23 wells report a pump yield, so the local sample is limited. The reported median yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 7.5 to 12.5 gallons per minute. Seventy percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Have the specific well tested and confirm its permitted use before planning irrigation or livestock demand.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Naturita?
faq.a: The available permit records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, there are 14 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 135 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. These are reasons to test the property’s water through a laboratory and review nearby environmental records before relying on it.

faq.q: Are there dry wells near Naturita, Colorado?
faq.a: The records show a wide depth range and mostly unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, which can make production unpredictable from lot to lot. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, but only 23 wells report yield and 169 are recorded as constructed out of 469 permits. Review neighboring construction reports and have a driller assess the parcel before buying.
